translations.text: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the Lord, saying, “Who will go up for us against the Canaanites, as a messenger to fight them for us?”
The Lord said to them, “Judah shall go up. Look, I have handed the land over to him.”
Judah said to his brother Simeon, “Come up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight the Canaanites. Then I too will go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up, and the Lord handed the Canaanites and the Perizzites over to him. They killed ten thousand men at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek and fought against him, and they killed the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him, followed him, and captured him. They cut off his thumbs and big toes.

Adoni-bezek said to them, “Seventy kings, whose thumbs and big toes had been cut off, used to gather food beneath my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me.” They took him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They struck it with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.
After this, the people of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the mountains.

Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, and the people of Hebron came out to confront them. Hebron was formerly called Kiriath-arba-sepher [?]. They killed Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.
From there they went against those who lived in Debir. Debir was formerly called the City of the Book.
Caleb said, “Whoever attacks the City of the Book and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife.

When she was about to leave, Othniel advised her to ask her father to give her a wooded garden. She groaned while sitting on the donkey and cried out from the donkey, saying, “You have sent me into the southern country.” Caleb said to her, “What is the matter with you?”
Achsah said to him, “Give me a blessing, since you have sent me into the southern country. Give me pools of water.” Caleb gave her, as her heart desired, a warm pool and a cold pool.

The descendants of Jobab the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up from the city of palms with the people of Judah into the countryside of Judah, toward the south, on the slopes of Arad. He went and lived among the people.
Judah went with his brother Simeon, and they killed the Canaanites who lived in Zephath. They devoted the city to destruction and destroyed it.
Judah did not take possession of Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, or Ashdod and its territory and outlying settlements.
The Lord was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country. But he could not dispossess those who lived in the lowlands, because they had iron chariots.
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said. He took possession of the cities there and drove the three sons of Anak out of that place.
The people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem. The Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin to this day.
The descendants of Joseph also went up to Bethel.
The city was formerly called Luz.
The scouts saw a man coming out of the city. They seized him and said to him, “Show us the entrance to the city, and we will treat you mercifully.”
He showed them where to enter the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword. But they let that man and his relatives go free.
The man went into the land of the Hittites and built a city there. He named it Luz, and that has been its name to this day.

Manasseh did not take possession of Beth-shean, the city of the Scythians, or its dependent towns or its settlements, or Ekdaad [?] and its dependent towns, or those who lived in Dor and its dependent towns, or those who lived in Bileam and its dependent towns, or those who lived in Megiddo and its dependent towns, or those who lived in Ibleam and its dependent towns. The Canaanites persisted in living in that land.
Afterward, when Israel became strong, they subjected the Canaanites to forced labor, but they did not destroy them completely.
And Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanites who lived in Gezer; the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer and became tributaries to them.
And Zebulun did not destroy those who lived in Kedron or those who lived in Aman; the Canaanites lived among them and became tributaries to them.

And Asher did not destroy those who lived in Acco, and they became tributaries to them, nor those who lived in Dor, nor those who lived in Sidon, nor those who lived in Dalaph, and Askod, and Kedia, and Aphek, and Rehob.
And Asher lived among the Canaanites who lived in that land, for they were unable to destroy them.

And Naphtali did not destroy those who lived in Beth-shemesh, nor those who lived in Betenet; and Israel lived among the Canaanites who were in that land, and those who lived in Beth-shemesh and in Betenek became tributaries to them.

And the Amorites pressed the children of Dan into the hill country, for they did not let them come down into the valleys. And the Amorites began to live on Mount Mersinon, where there are bears and foxes; but the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed over the Amorites, and they became tributaries to them.
And the mountain of the Amorites belonged to the Edomites, the upper part of Akrabbim, which are upon the rock.

And the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Klauthmon, and to Bethel, and to the house of Israel. And the Lord said to them: "I brought you out of Egypt and brought you into the land which I swore to your fathers to give you, and I said to you, 'I will never forsake my covenant with you.'

"And you, do not make a covenant with those who live in this land, nor with their gods, and do not bow down to them; smash their carved images and tear down their altars. But you did not listen to my voice when you did this."
"So I too said: I will no longer remove the peoples whom I said I would drive out from before you; they will become a grief to you, and their gods will become a stumbling block to you."
Then, when the angel of the Lord spoke these words to all Israel, all the people cried out and wept.
And because of this the name of that place was called Weeping, and they offered sacrifice there to the Lord.
And he dismissed the people, and all the children of Israel went back to their houses and to their inheritance, to take possession of the land.

And the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders whose days were prolonged after Joshua, all who had known all the great work of the Lord which he had done for Israel.
And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, being a hundred and ten years old.
And they buried him on the mountain of his inheritance, in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north side of Mount Gaash.
And that whole generation went to their fathers, and another generation arose after them, all of whom did not know the Lord or the work which he had done for Israel.
And the children of Israel did evil before the Lord and served the Baals.

And they forsook the Lord, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, and followed other gods, the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them, and provoked the Lord to anger.
And they forsook the Lord and served Baal and Astarte.

And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he handed them over to those who would take them captive; and they took them captive and carried them off into the land of their enemies who were around them, and they could not stand before their enemies in all the ways those plundered them.
And the hand of the Lord was against them for evil, as the Lord had said and as the Lord had sworn, and they afflicted them greatly.
The Lord raised up judges, and the Lord saved them from the hands of those who had taken them captive.

Yet they did not listen even to their judges, for they prostituted themselves, followed other gods, and bowed down to them. They provoked the Lord to anger and quickly abandoned the path their ancestors had followed in obeying the word of the Lord. They did not do as their ancestors had done.

Whenever the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with that judge and saved them from the hands of their enemies throughout that judge’s lifetime. For the Lord had compassion on them because of the suffering they endured at the hands of those who fought against them.

But when that judge died, they would turn back again and become more corrupt than their ancestors. They would go after other gods, worship them, and bow down to them. They would not abandon their wickedness or turn back from their evil way.
The Lord’s anger burned against Israel, and he said, “Because this people of mine has abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors to keep, and has not obeyed my voice,
I, in turn, will no longer drive out before them a single man from the nations that Joshua left behind.”
He left them to test Israel through them, to see whether they would keep the way of the Lord and walk in it as their ancestors had kept it, or not.
The Lord left these nations and did not drive them out quickly or hand them over to Joshua.
The Lord left these nations to test through them all those Israelites who had not known any of the wars of Canaan.
This was for the sake of the generations of the Israelites, so that they might teach them warfare, though those before them had not known it either.
These five peoples of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath.
They remained so that he might test Israel through them, to find out whether they would obey the commandment of the Lord, which he had commanded their ancestors through Moses.
The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
They took their daughters as wives and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they worshiped their gods.
The Israelites did evil in the Lord’s sight. They forgot the Lord their God and worshiped the Baals and their images.
The Lord’s anger burned against Israel, and he handed them over to Cushan-rishathaim, king of Syria of Mesopotamia of the Rivers. The Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim for eight years.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for Israel, who saved them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother. They obeyed him.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to battle, and the Lord handed Cushan-rishathaim, king of Syria, over to him.
The land had rest for fifty years, and Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did evil in the Lord’s sight, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel because they had done evil in the Lord’s sight.
He gathered all the Ammonites and Amalekites against them, went and slaughtered the Israelites, and took possession of the city of palms.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud son of Gera, a Benjaminite, a man equally skilled with either hand. The Israelites sent tribute with him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a double-edged dagger a span long and strapped it beneath his belt at his right hip.
He brought his tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
When Ehud had finished presenting his tribute, he sent away those who had carried it.
Eglon returned from the temple of the gods at Gilgal, and Ehud said to him, “I have a message for you alone, O king.” Eglon commanded everyone to leave him, and all those attending him went out.
Ehud came in to him while he was sitting alone in his upper room, and it was summer. Ehud said to him, “I have something to tell you, O king.” Eglon rose from his seat, and Ehud approached him.
When he rose, Ehud raised his left hand, drew his sword from his right side, and thrust it into Eglon's belly.
He drove it into him as far as the hilt and pierced him through to his back. Then he drew the sword out of his belly.
Ehud went out into the porch, closed the doors of the upper room behind him, and bolted them.

After he had gone out, Eglon's servants came in, looked, and found the door of the upper chamber locked. They said, "Perhaps he is sitting alone and silent in the inner room of his upper chamber [?]."
They waited until they were embarrassed, but no one opened the doors of the upper room for them. They took the key and opened them, and found their master lying dead on the ground.
But Ehud escaped while they were confused, and no one noticed him. He passed beyond their idols and escaped to Seirah.
Then, when he reached the land of Israel, he blew a horn in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down from the hills with him, and he went ahead of them.

He said to them, "Come down and follow me, for the Lord has delivered our enemies, the Moabites, into our hands." They went down and followed him, reached the crossings of the Jordan leading to Moab, and allowed no one to cross.
In those days they killed about ten thousand Moabite men, all warriors and all men of great strength. None of them escaped, not even one man.
In those days Moab came under the power of Israel, and the land rested for eighty years. Ehud judged them until he died.
After this, Shamgar son of Anath arose and killed six hundred Philistine men with an ox goad. He too delivered [Israel].
The Israelites again did evil before the Lord, and Ehud had died.
The Lord delivered them into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the nations.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, because Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots, and he afflicted Israel, oppressing them for twenty (and five) years.
Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel in those days.
Deborah used to sit by the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites went up to her to have their cases judged.

Deborah sent for Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and summoned him. She said to him, “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you to go to Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun?”
"I will bring you to the river Kishon against Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his multitude, and I will deliver him into your hands."
Barak said to her, "If you go with me, I will go. But if you do not go with me, I will not go, because I do not know the day on which the Lord intends to send his angel with me."

Deborah said to him, “I will go with you. But know that, on the journey you are taking, it will not be as you first said, for the Lord will hand Sisera over to a woman.” Deborah got up and went with Barak from Kedesh.
Barak summoned Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh, and ten thousand men went up with him. Deborah also went up with him.
Those related to Kenaz separated from the descendants of Hobab, Moses' father-in-law, and his camp settled by the tree of Lebaith, near Kedesh.
They informed Sisera that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor.
Sisera brought all his chariots—for he had nine hundred iron chariots—and all his troops from Harosheth of the Nations to the Kishon River.

Deborah said to Barak, "Rise, for this is the day on which the Lord will deliver Sisera into your hands. Look, the Lord is going ahead of you!" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor, with ten thousand men following him.
The Lord threw Sisera, all his chariots, and his entire army into panic, bringing them down before Barak by the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak pursued the chariots and chased the army as far as the field of the nations. Sisera's entire army died by the sword; not even one remained.
Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber, the other Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin, king of [Hazor], and the household of Heber the Kenite.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord, turn aside to me. Do not be afraid." He turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with sackcloth.
Sisera said to her, “Give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.” She opened a skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered his face.
He said to her, “Stand at the entrance to the tent. If anyone comes to you and asks, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” Then she covered him with sackcloth.

Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg and a stone in her other hand and went in to him. She struck him and drove the peg into his jaw, piercing him until she pinned him to the ground. He struggled between her feet, stretched out, and died.

Barak arrived, pursuing Sisera. Jael came out to meet Barak and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” He went in with her and found Sisera lying dead, with the peg in his jaw.
That day God humbled Jabin, king of Canaan, before the Israelites.
The hand of God advanced with the Israelites and grew ever stronger against Jabin, king of Canaan, until he destroyed him.
Deborah and Barak sang that day, and she said as she sang:
“When the rulers of Israel took the lead, with the willing resolve of the people, let them bless the Lord.
Listen, kings! Pay attention, mighty rulers! I will sing to the Lord, the God of Israel.
Lord, when you went out from Seir, when you arose from the country of Edom, the earth shook, heaven trembled, and the clouds dripped water.
The mountains shook before the Lord, this Sinai before the Lord, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, kings disappeared, and those who traveled the roads went by crooked paths.
The champions disappeared from Israel; they disappeared until Deborah arose, until she stood as a mother to Israel.
They delighted in worthless gods, like barley bread when they cover it while it is hot. Spears—forty thousand spears. [?]
My heart is with those who command Israel, with Israel’s mighty men. Bless the Lord!
You who ride on white donkeys and sit in the light, speak out!
Take provisions among those who rejoice. There they acknowledge the Lord’s righteousness, and the righteousness he established in Israel. At that time the Lord’s people went down into his towns.

Arise, Deborah, and raise up thousands with the people! Arise, arise with a song! Arise in strength, Barak! Deborah, strengthen Barak! Lead away your captives, Barak son of Abinoam, as on the day when his strength became great.
Lord, weaken for me those who overpower me.

The people of Ephraim struck them in the valleys; your brother Benjamin was among your people. From me, Machir, they came down to test [?]; and from Zebulun the Lord fights for me, and from the mighty men there, with the rod of the power of speech. [?]

And from Issachar, with Deborah, he sent his foot soldiers into the valleys, so that you might sit between the edges [?]. And he spread out at his feet [?] Reuben; great was the searching of his heart.
Why do you sit in Mesopotamia, listening as those who rise to cross into Zerobel dispute with one another? [?]
Great was the resolve of Gilead’s heart; he remained beyond the Jordan. And Dan—why does he remain among the ships? Asher stayed by the seashore and remained within his borders.
Zebulun was a people who exposed their lives to death, and Naphtali on the heights of the open country.
Kings came and fought. At that time the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo, but they took no silver as plunder.
The stars fought in heaven; from their [?] they fought against Sisera.
The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river; the River Kishon killed him. Be strong, my soul!
Then the hooves of their horses were battered by their galloping [?].
His mighty men curse Meroz. The angel of the Lord said, ‘Utterly curse those within its houses, because they did not come to the Lord’s aid against the mighty warriors.’
Blessed above women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed above women in the tent.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk; in a large bowl she brought him curds.
With her left hand she reached for a tent peg, and with her right a hammer. She killed Sisera and crushed his head and smashed his jaw.
He collapsed between her feet, and where he collapsed, there he was brought low.

Sisera’s mother peered through the window, looking through the lattice to see whether anyone had returned from Sisera. “Why is Sisera’s chariot so late in arriving? Why are the steps of his chariots delayed?”
Her wise messengers answered her; they answered her in keeping with her own words.

“Have they not found him dividing the plunder, while his companions contend over the heads of the warriors? Sisera has plundered colored cloth, he has plundered colored cloth; each has [?] of its colors, and he has hung what he plundered around his neck.”
So may all your enemies perish, Lord! But may those who love you be like the sun rising in its strength. And the land rested for forty years.
The Israelites did evil before the Lord, and the Lord handed them over to Midian for seven years.
The Midianites gained power over Israel, and because of Midian the Israelites made caves and strongholds for themselves in the mountains and among the cliffs.
Whenever the people of Israel sowed their crops, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the people of the east would come up against them.
They would camp against them and destroy the produce of their fields as far as Gaza. They left Israel nothing to live on, neither their flocks nor their cattle nor their donkeys.

For they came up against them with their livestock, bringing their tents. They arrived in numbers like locusts; neither they nor their camels could be counted. They came into the land of Israel to devastate it.
Israel became very poor because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the Lord.
When the Israelites cried out to the Lord because of Midian,
the Lord sent a prophet to the Israelites, who told them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I am the one who brought you out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
I rescued you from the power of the Egyptians and from all who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
I told you, ‘I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of these Amorites in whose land you live.’ But you did not obey my voice.”

The angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the tree at Ephrathah that belonged to Joash, the father of Abiezer. His son Gideon was beating out wheat on his threshing floor to hide it from the Midianites.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “The Lord is with you, mighty warrior.”

Gideon said to him, “Oh, sir, my lord! If the Lord is with us, why has all this trouble happened to us? Where are all his glorious deeds that our fathers told us about? They told us, ‘The Lord brought our fathers out of Egypt.’ But now the Lord has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian.”
The angel of the Lord looked at him and said, “Go in your strength and save Israel from the power of Midian. Look, I have sent you.”
Gideon said to him, “Oh, my lord, how can I save Israel? Look, my clan is small in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s household.”
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Because the Lord is with you, you will strike down the Midianites as though they were one man.”
Gideon said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, give me a sign that you are the one speaking with me.
Do not leave here until I return to you, bring my offering, and set it before you.” He said to him, “I am the one, and I will wait for you until you return.”
Gideon went and prepared a young goat and unleavened loaves. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, brought them to him under the tree, and bowed down to him.
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread, put them on the rock, and pour out the broth.” And he did so.

The angel of the Lord raised his staff and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire blazed up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread. Then the angel of the Lord disappeared from his sight.
Gideon realized that he was the angel of the Lord. Gideon said, “Alas, Lord! I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face!”
The Lord said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid. You will not die.”
Gideon built an altar to the Lord there and called it “The Peace of the Lord.” It remains to this day in Ephrathah of the father of Ezri.
Then, that night, the Lord said to him, “Take your father’s fattened bull and a second bull, seven years old. Tear down your father’s altar to Baal, and break the image above it.
Build an altar there to the Lord your God, who appeared to you on Mount Maok in this region. Take the second bull and offer it as a sacrifice using the wood you have broken.”
Gideon took thirteen men from among his servants and did as the Lord had told him. Because he was afraid of his father’s household and the men of his town, he went in at night rather than by day.
The men of the town rose early in the morning and found Baal’s altar torn down, the image above it broken, and the fattened bull offered as a sacrifice on the altar that had been built.
They said to one another, “Who did this?” They searched and questioned people, and they said, “Gideon son of Joash did this.”
The men of the town said to Joash, “Bring out your son so that they may kill him, because he tore down Baal’s altar and broke the image above it.”

Joash said to the men who stood against him, “Will you now take vengeance for Baal? Or will you save him by killing the one who wronged him? If he is a god, let the one who wronged him die by morning, and let him himself take vengeance on the one who tore down his altar.”
He named him Awd-Baal that day, because he had torn down his altar.
All the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the people of the east gathered together against him. They crossed over and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.
The Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon. He blew a horn, and Abiezer rallied behind him.
He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, and Manasseh also rallied behind him. He sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
Gideon said to the Lord, “If you will save Israel through my hand, as you have said,

look, I will spread a large amount of wool on the threshing floor. If dew falls on the wool alone while all the ground is dry, then I will know that you will save Israel through my hand, as you have said.”
And it happened that way. Gideon rose early and squeezed the wool. Water came out of the wool and filled a basin.
Gideon said to the Lord, “Do not be angry with me in your wrath. Let me speak to you once more: let the wool alone be dry, and let dew fall on all the ground.”
The Lord did so that night. The wool alone was dry, and dew fell on all the ground.

Rehoboam [?], who was Gideon, rose early with all the people who were with him, and they camped in the land of Harod. The camp of Midian and Amalek was to the north of the altar of [?], in the valley.
The Lord said to Gideon, “The people with you are too many for me to hand Midian over to them, lest Israel boast against me and say, ‘My own hand saved me.’”

The Lord said to him, “Tell the people, ‘Whoever among you is afraid and fearful, let him return from among the people.’” They turned back from Mount Gilead, and twenty-two thousand of the people returned, while ten thousand remained.
The Lord said to Gideon, “There are still too many people. Bring them down to the water, and I will test them for you there. Those whom I tell you about shall go with you.”
He brought the people down to the water. The Lord said to Gideon, “Set apart everyone who drinks water with his tongue as a dog drinks, and set apart everyone who kneels on his knees to drink.”
The number of those who drank with their tongues was three hundred men. The rest of the people knelt on their knees to drink water.
The Lord said to Gideon, “Through these three hundred men who drank this way, I will save you and deliver Midian into your hand. Let all the people go home.”
They took the people’s provisions and their horns with them. He sent all the men of Israel away to go home, but kept those three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below them in the valley.
Then that night the Lord said to him, “Get up! Go down quickly from here into the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand.”
“But if you are afraid to go down alone, go down into the camp with your servant Purah.”
“Listen to what they are saying. Then your hands will be strengthened, and you can go down into the camp.” So he and his servant Purah went down to one company of fifty in the camp.
Midian, Amalek, and all the people of the east were encamped in the valleys, as numerous as locusts. Their camels were beyond counting, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

Gideon came, and there was a man telling his companion his dream. He said to him, “I had a dream, and I saw a loaf of barley bread rolling into the camp of Midian. It struck it, and it fell; it overturned it from above, and the camp collapsed.”
The other man answered him, “This is nothing but the spear of Gideon son of Joash, a man of Israel. God has handed Midian and their whole camp over to him.”

Then, when Gideon heard the interpretation of the dream and the account of the dream, he bowed down to God. He returned to the camp of Israel and said to them, “Get up, for the Lord has delivered the camp of Midian into our hands.”
He divided the three hundred men into three companies and put a horn into each man’s hand, along with new jars and torches inside the jars.
He said to them, “Watch me and do the same. Look, I am going into the middle of the camp. Do as I do.”
“When I and everyone with me blow the horn, you too must blow your horns all around the camp and say, ‘For the Lord and for Gideon!’”
Gideon and the hundred men with him entered one section of the camp at the first hour of the middle of the night, before the guards awoke. They blew their horns and smashed the jars in their hands.

The three companies blew their horns and smashed their jars. They raised the torches in their left hands, while in their right hands they held the horns they were blowing. They shouted, “The battle of the Lord and of Gideon!”
They all stood in their places around the camp. Everyone in the camp ran and panicked.

They blew the three hundred horns, and throughout the camp the Lord turned each man’s sword against his companion. Their forces fled as far as Beth-shittah, and as many as a thousand gathered at Abel-meholah and Gabaoth.
The men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh raised a battle cry and pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout the territory of Ephraim, saying, “Come down to meet the Midianites and intercept them at the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim were called out, and they reached the waters ahead of them, as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.

They captured the two leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at Surin and Zeeb at Iaphec, and they pursued Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon from beyond the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim said to him, “What is this you have done to us, not calling us when you went to fight Midian?” They argued fiercely with him.
He said to them, “What have I done now that compares with what you have done? Are not Ephraim’s gleanings better than Abiezer’s harvest?”

“Did not the Lord deliver the leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, into your hands? What have I been able to do compared with you?” Then they left him alone, and their anger toward him subsided when he said these words to them.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed it, he and the two hundred men with him. They grew faint when they were hungry.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Give food to the people with me, because they are hungry, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
The officials of Succoth said to him, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give food to your army?”
Gideon said to them, “Not so! When the Lord delivers Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will impale your flesh on wilderness thorns and briers.”
He went up from there to Penuel [and spoke to them in the same way, and they answered him] as the people of Succoth had answered him.
He said to the people of Penuel, “When I return safely, I will tear down this tower.”

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, with their army of about fifteen thousand—all who remained of the entire army of the people of the east. Those who had fallen numbered one hundred and two thousand men who carried weapons.
Gideon went up by the road of the easterners who lived in enclosures toward Nobah, above Zebah, and attacked their army while they felt secure.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and followed them. He captured both kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and Gideon crushed their entire army.
Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.
They captured a young man from among the people of Succoth, and he questioned him. He had him write down the officials of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

He came [to the officials of] Succoth and said to them, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, over whom you mocked me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give food to your hungry men?’”
He took the people of Succoth, their elders and their officials, and impaled them on wilderness thorns and briers. Along with them he impaled the people of Succoth.
He tore down the tower of Penuel and struck down the people of Penuel and their city.
He said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “Where are the men you killed at Tabor?” They said to him, “They were like you. They resembled you, with the appearance of kings’ sons.”
Gideon said to them, “They were my brothers, my mother’s sons.” He swore to them, saying, “As the Lord lives, if you had kept them alive, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the boy did not draw his sword, because he was young and afraid.

Zebah and Zalmunna said to him, “Get up yourself and confront us, for your strength is that of a man.” Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments from their camels’ necks.
The people of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, you and your children, because you have saved us from the hand of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you. The Lord will rule over you.”
Gideon said to them, “I ask one thing of you: each of you, give me the gold earrings he took as plunder.” For they had many earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.
They said, “We will gladly give them.” He spread out his garment, and each man threw onto it the earrings he had plundered.

The weight of the gold earrings he had requested from them was nineteen hundred shekels of gold, apart from the pendants, the crescent ornaments of the ephod, the purple cloaks worn by the kings of Midian, and the gold chains around their camels’ necks.

Gideon made an image for himself and set it up in his city, in Ephraim. All Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it and followed it there. It became a cause of sin for Gideon and his household.
Midian was humbled before Israel, and they never again raised their heads. The land rested for forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jeroboam son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons who went about at his side, for he had many wives.
His concubine in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died in the town of Seneth and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
After Gideon died, the Israelites turned back and followed the Baals, and they made a covenant with Baal to be their god.
The Israelites did not remember the Lord their God, who had saved them from the hands of all their enemies around them.
They showed no kindness to the household of Jeroboam, who was Gideon, in return for all the good he had done for Israel.
Abimelech son of Rehoboam went to Shechem, to his mother's brothers, and spoke to all the relatives of his mother's household.

He said to them, "Speak on my behalf to the people of Shechem and ask them, ‘Which is better for you: for seventy men—all the sons of Rehoboam—to rule you, or for one man to rule you? Remember that I am your own flesh and bone.’"
His mother's brothers spoke all these words on his behalf to all the people of Shechem. They turned their hearts toward Abimelech and said, "He is our brother."
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal. With these, Abimelech hired reckless men and troublemakers, who went and followed him.
He entered his father's house in Ephraim and killed his brothers, the sons of Rehoboam, seventy men, on a single stone. But Jotham, Rehoboam's youngest son, survived because he had hidden himself.
All the people of Shechem and all of Beth-millo gathered together. They went and made Abimelech their king beside the oak tree in Shechem.
They told Jotham, and he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. He shouted and wept and said to them, "Listen to me, people of Shechem, and may God listen to you.
The trees went out to appoint a king for themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
The olive tree said to them, ‘Should I give up my oil, for which God and human beings have honored me, and go to reign over the trees?’
All the trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come, reign over us.’
The fig tree said to them, ‘Should I give up my sweetness and my blessed fruit and go to reign over the trees?’
All the trees said to the vine, “Come, reign over us.”
The vine said to them, ‘Should I give up my wine and the joy I bring to God and human beings, and go to reign over the trees?’
The trees said to the thornbush, ‘You come and reign over us.’
The thornbush said to them, ‘If you truly and rightly appoint me king over you, come and take shelter under my shade. If not, let fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’
Now, if you have acted truly and rightly in making Abimelech king, in how you have treated Jeroboam and his household, and if you have treated him as the deeds of his hands deserved—
for my father fought for you, risked his life for you, and saved you from the hands of Midian—

yet you rose up against my father's household and killed his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his concubine, king over the people of Shechem because he is your brother.
If, then, you have acted faithfully and uprightly toward Rehoboam and his household this day, you too are blessed. Rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.
But if not, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume the people of Shechem and Beth-millo, and let fire come out of the people of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech."
Jotham fled, ran along the road, and escaped to Rara. He stayed there to keep away from his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech ruled over the house of Israel for three years.
God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and the people of Shechem betrayed the house of Abimelech,

so that the guilt for the seventy sons of Jeroboam and their blood would come back and be repaid to their brother Abimelech, who had killed them, and to the people of Shechem, who had strengthened his hand to kill his brothers.
The people of Shechem set an ambush for him on the mountaintops, and they robbed everyone who passed along the road above them. Abimelech was told about this.
Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers came to Shechem, and the men of Shechem joined him.
They went out into the fields, gathered the grapes from their vineyards, trod them, and held a festival. They entered the house of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is the son of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Rehoboam, and is not Zebul his overseer? Serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem! Why should we serve him?
If only someone would put these people into my hands! Then I would drive Abimelech out, and I would say to Abimelech, ‘Increase your forces and come out!’”
Zebul, the governor of the city, heard what Gaal son of Ebed had said, and he became furious.
He sent messengers to Abimelech with a gift, saying, “Look, Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem, and now they are stirring up the city against you.
Now get up during the night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush in the fields.
In the morning, when the sun rises, advance and attack the city.”
He and the people with him came during the night and lay in ambush against Shechem in four companies.
When morning came, Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance to the city gate. Abimelech and the people with him rose from their ambush.
Gaal son of Ebed saw the people and said to Zebul, “Look, people are coming down from the mountaintop!” Zebul said to him, “You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as though they were people.”
Gaal spoke again and said to him, “Look, people are coming down toward the sea from the center of the land, and one company is coming along the road of [?].”
Zebul said to him, “Where is that mouth of yours now, with which you said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Are these not the people you mocked? Go out now and fight them!”
Gaal went out at the head of the men of Shechem and fought Abimelech.
Abimelech pursued him, and he fled before him. Many fell and were killed as far as the city gate.
Abimelech stayed in Arumah. Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers and prevented them from living in Shechem.
Then, on the next day, the people went out into the open country, and Abimelech was told.
He took his people, divided them into three companies, and lay in ambush with them. As he watched, he saw the people coming out of the city. He rose against them and killed them.
Abimelech and the company with him took their stand [?] at the entrance to the city gate, while the other two companies spread out through all the open country and killed them.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. They captured the city, and he killed the people inside it and sowed it with salt.
All the people of the tower of Shechem heard about it and entered the stronghold of the house of Baal.
Abimelech was told that all the people of the tower of Shechem had gathered together.

Abimelech went up Mount Hermon, he and the people with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand, cut a load of wood, lifted it, and carried it on his shoulders. He said to the people with him, “What you have seen me do, do yourselves quickly, just as I have done.”

They too all cut their loads of wood, picked them up, and followed Abimelech. They laid them against the stronghold and set their stronghold on fire over them. All the people of Shechem who were in the tower died, about a thousand men and women.
Abimelech went to Thebez. They laid siege to it and captured it.
There was a large tower in the middle of the city. They all took refuge there—their men and women and all the leading men of the city. They shut themselves in and went up onto the roof of the tower.
Abimelech went to the tower, and they fought against it. Abimelech approached the entrance of the tower to burn it with fire.
A woman threw a piece of a millstone at Abimelech's head and crushed his jaw.

He quickly called to the young man who carried his weapons and said to him, “Draw your sword and kill me, so that people will not say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” His young man stabbed him, and Abimelech died.
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went back to their homes.
God repaid Abimelech for the evil he had done against his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God brought all the evil of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads, and the curse of Jotham son of Rehoboam came upon them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, the son of his father's brother, a man of Issachar, arose to save Israel. He lived in Samaria, in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Samaria.
After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty-two sons who rode thirty-two donkeys. They had thirty-two towns, which he named the Villages of Jair, as they are called to this day. They are in Gilead.
Jair died and was buried in Ramo.

The Israelites again did evil before the Lord. They worshiped the Baals and Ashtoreth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the Lord and did not serve him.
The Lord's anger flared against Israel, and he handed them over to the Philistines and the Ammonites.
They tormented and crushed the Israelites beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites in Gilead.
The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim. The Israelites suffered greatly.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord and said, “We have sinned against you, because we abandoned you, our God, and worshiped the Baals.”
The Lord said to the Israelites, “Was it not Egypt, the Amorites, the Ammonites, Moab, and the Philistines,
“and Sidon, Midian, and Amalek who oppressed you? You cried out to me, and I saved you from their hands.
“But you abandoned me and worshiped other gods. Because of this, I will not save you.”
“Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen for yourselves, and let them save you in your days of distress.”
The Israelites said to the Lord, “We have sinned. Do to us whatever you wish. Only save us today, Lord!”
They removed the foreign gods from among them, worshiped the Lord, and pleased him; and they [?] from the suffering of Israel.
The Ammonites went up and camped in Gilead. The Israelites went out and camped in the land of Mizpah.
The messengers of the people of Gilead said to one another, “Who is the man who will begin fighting the Ammonites for us? Let him become the head of everyone who lives in Gilead.”
Jephthah the Gileadite was strong and mighty. He was the son of a prostitute, who bore Jephthah to Gilead.

[His freeborn wife] bore sons to Gilead. When that woman's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, “You will not inherit anything in our father's house, because you are the son of another woman.”
Jephthah went away from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Poor men gathered around Jephthah and went about with him.
After some time, the Ammonites fought against Israel.
The elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, “Come and be our commander, so that we may fight the Ammonites.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Was it not you who hated me and drove me out of my father’s house and away from you? Why, then, have you come to me now, when you are in distress?”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “No, it is not so. We have come to you so that you may go with us and fight the Ammonites for us, and become our head over everyone who lives in Gilead.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “If you take me with you to fight the Ammonites, then, when the Lord delivers them before me, I will become your head.”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The Lord is our witness between us that we will do just as you have said.”
Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people appointed him as their head, to be their ruler. Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What do you have against me, that you come to fight me in my land?”

The king of the Ammonites said to those whom Jephthah had sent, “Because Israel took my land when they came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and as far as the Jordan. Now return it to me peacefully.” Those whom Jephthah had sent returned to him.
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites.
He said to him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take your land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites when they came up from Egypt.
“Instead, Israel traveled through the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and reached Kadesh.”
“Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Let me pass through your land.’ But the king of Edom refused. Israel also sent to the king of Moab, and he refused. So Israel stayed in Kadesh.”

They passed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab. They reached the eastern side of the land of Moab and camped beyond the Arnon. They did not enter the territory of Moab, because the Arnon was Moab’s boundary.
Israel sent messengers to Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon. Israel said to him, “Let me pass through your land to my own country.”
Sihon refused to let Israel pass through his territory. Sihon gathered his people, camped at Jazer, and fought against Israel.
The Lord, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into Israel’s hands, and they killed them. Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived in that land.
They took possession of all the Amorites’ territory, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now the Lord, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before Israel, and will you take possession of it by force?
Do you not take possession of what Chemosh your god has given you? Likewise, we will take possession of everything that the Lord our God has given us before us.
Now, are you better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel or wage war against the house of Israel?
In Heshbon and its dependent towns, in Jazer and its dependent towns, and in all the towns near the Jordan, for three hundred years—why did they not recover them during that time?
I have not wronged you, but you are doing me wrong by fighting against me. May the Lord, who judges, judge today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.”
The king of the Ammonites refused them and did not listen to the message Jephthah sent him.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He crossed through the land of Gilead and Manasseh, and crossed through the territory of Gilead, and from the territory of Gilead he crossed over to the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the Lord and said, “If you deliver the Ammonites into my hands—”
“Whoever comes out through the door of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites, I will make a sacrifice to the Lord.”
Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight them, and the Lord delivered them into his hands.
He killed them from Aroer as far as Emoith, twenty towns, and as far as Abel of the Vineyards—a very great slaughter. The Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites.

Jephthah entered his house at Mizpah, and there was his daughter coming out to meet him with a tambourine and a lyre. She was his only child, whom he loved; he had no other child besides her, neither son nor daughter.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me low and have become a source of anguish in my eyes. I have opened my mouth to the Lord concerning you, and it cannot be revoked.”
She said to him, “Father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord concerning me, do to me what you have said, for the Lord has given you vengeance on your enemies, the Ammonites.”
She said to her father, “Do this one thing for me: allow me two months to go up into the mountains and mourn my virginity with my companions.”
He said to her, “Go,” and sent her away for two months. She went with her companions and mourned her virginity with them in the mountains.
After the two months had ended, she returned to her father, and Jephthah carried out the vow he had made. She had never had sexual relations with a man. And it became a custom in Israel.
Each year, at the time of her anniversary, the daughters of Israel would go to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days.
The Ephraimites gathered and came to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why did you go to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down over you!”
Jephthah said to them, “I was a wronged man, as were my people. The Ammonites oppressed us severely. We cried out to you, but you did not save us from their hands.”

“When I saw that there was no one to save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the Lord delivered them into my hands. Why have you come up against me today to fight me?”
Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead killed the Ephraimites because they had said to them, “You are fugitives from Ephraim.”

The men of Gilead overtook them in the midst of Manasseh, at the Jordan crossings belonging to Ephraim. Then, when the fugitives of Ephraim said, “Let us cross,” the men of Gilead asked them, “Are you also from Ephraim?” They said, “No.”
They said to them, “Say ‘Womb,’” but they refused to say it. They seized them and killed them at the crossings of the Jordan. Forty-two thousand from Ephraim fell at that time.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his town in Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He married his daughters to men from outside and took thirty women from outside as wives for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel. He judged Israel for ten years.
Elon the Zebulunite died in Elon, and they buried him in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Lebon the Ephrathite judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Elon, the Ephrathite, died, and they buried him in Ephrath, in the land of Ephraim, on Mount Leneq.
The Israelites again did evil before the Lord, and he delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, whose name was Manoah. His wife was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the Lord appeared to his wife and said to her, “Look, you are barren and have not borne a child, but you will conceive and bear a son.”
“Now be careful: do not drink wine or mead, and do not eat anything unclean.”

“For you will conceive and bear a son, and no iron blade shall touch his head, because the child will be holy, a Nazirite dedicated to the Lord from his mother’s womb. He will begin to save Israel from the hands of the Philistines.”

The woman went and told her husband, saying, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like that of an angel of the Lord, and he was very awe-inspiring. I asked him where he was from, but he did not tell me his name.”

“He said to me, ‘You will conceive and bear a son. Now do not drink wine or mead, and do not eat anything unclean, because the child will be a Nazirite dedicated to the Lord from his mother’s womb until the day he dies.’”
Manoah prayed to the Lord and said, “Lord, let the man of God whom you sent to us come to us and teach us what we should do for the child who will be born.”
The Lord heard Manoah’s words, and the angel of the Lord came again to his wife while she was sitting in the open country. Manoah, her husband, was not with her.
The woman ran quickly and told her husband, saying, “Look, the man who came to me before has appeared to me.”
Manoah got up and followed his wife to the man. He said to him, “Are you the man who spoke with my wife?” The angel answered him, “I am.”
Manoah said to him, “Now, when your word comes true, what will be the rule for the child, and what will his work be?”
The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “You must observe everything I told your wife.
He must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. You must observe everything I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “Let us entertain you and prepare a young goat for you here in your presence.”
The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Even if you entertain me, I will not eat your food. But if you make a sacrifice to the Lord, make it to him.”
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “What is your name, so that we may honor you when your word comes true?”
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Why do you ask my name? It is wonderful.”
Manoah took a young goat and an offering and offered them on a rock to the Lord, who performs wonders for the Lord. Manoah and his wife watched as the flame rose from above the altar into heaven.
The angel of the Lord ascended into heaven in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife saw him and fell facedown on the ground.
The angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to his wife, “We will certainly die, because we have seen God.”

His wife said to him, “If the Lord had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted our sacrifice and our offering from our hands. He would not have shown us all this, nor would he have let us hear this at such a time.”
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The Lord blessed him, and the child grew.
The Spirit of the Lord began to go with him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a woman there among the daughters of the Philistines. She pleased him.
He went up and told his father and mother, saying, “I have seen a woman in Timnah among the daughters of the Philistines. Now get her for me as a wife.”

His father and mother said to him, “Is there no woman among the daughters of your relatives or among all my people, that you must go and take a wife from the daughters of the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “But get her for me, because she is pleasing in my eyes.”
His father and mother did not know that this was from the Lord, because he was seeking vengeance against the Philistines. In those days the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. He turned aside into the vineyards of Timnah, and suddenly a lion came toward him, roaring.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he tore the lion apart as one tears apart a young goat, although he had nothing in his hands. He did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
They went up and spoke about the woman, and she pleased Samson.
After some days he returned to take her as his wife. He turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass, and there were bees settled in the lion’s mouth, and there was honey.
He took it and ate, walking along as he ate. He came to his father and mother and gave them some, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s mouth.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson stayed there for seven days, for that was how young men used to stay.
Then, because they were afraid of him, they appointed thirty companions for him, and they stayed with him.

Samson said to them, “I will pose a riddle to you. If you explain my riddle to me during these seven days of the feast and find its answer, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.
But if you cannot explain it to me, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.” They said to him, “Pose your riddle, and we will listen.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they could not explain his riddle.

Then, on the fourth day, they said to Samson’s wife, “Coax your husband into telling you his riddle, so that we do not burn you and your father’s household with fire. Or did you invite us here to make us poor?”

Samson’s wife wept before him and said to him, “You hate me and do not love me, because you have not told me the riddle you posed to my people.” Samson said to her, “Look, I have not told my father or my mother. Should I then tell you?”
She wept before him during the seven days of the feast. Then, on the seventh day, he told her because she had worn him down, and she explained it to her people.

On the seventh day, before the sun set, those men said to him, “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” Samson said to them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found the answer to my riddle.”

The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men. He stripped them of their clothes and gave them to those who had explained his riddle. Samson’s anger blazed, and he went to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife lived with his companion, who had been his wedding attendant.
Some time later, during the wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife and brought her a young goat. He said, “I will go in to my wife in her room.” But her father prevented him from going in to her.
Her father said to him, “Because you said, ‘I hate her,’ I gave her to your companion. But here is her sister, who is younger and prettier. Let her be yours instead.”
Samson said, “This time I am blameless toward the Philistines, for I will do you harm.”
Samson went and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches and tied the foxes by their tails, placing one torch between each pair of tails.

He lit the torches and released the foxes into the Philistines’ fields. They burned the grain, the heaps of harvested grain, the standing grain, and what was spread out, as well as the vineyards and olive groves.

The Philistines said, “Who did this?” They were told, “Samson, the Timnite’s son-in-law, because they took his wife away from him and gave her to his companion.” The Philistines went up and burned her father’s house, along with her and her father.
Samson said to them, “If you have done this, it is not right. I would take my revenge on one and all of you.”
Samson struck them on the joints of their legs, and there was a great slaughter. Then Samson went down and stayed in the ravine, in the cave of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah, and they arrayed themselves at Lehi.
All the people of Judah said to them, “Why have you come up against us?” The Philistines said, “We have come up to bind Samson and do to him as he did to us.”

Three thousand men from Judah went down to the cave in the rock at Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?” Samson said to them, “As they did to you, so I did to them.”

They said to him, “We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Swear to me that you yourselves will not kill me. Hand me over to them, but do not attack me yourselves.”
They swore to him and said, “No, we will only bind you with ropes and hand you over to them. We certainly will not kill you.” They bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from that rock.

When he reached Lehi, the Philistines shouted, came to meet him, and rushed at him. The Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and the ropes around his arms became like straw consumed by fire. His bonds came loose from his arms.
He found a donkey’s jawbone lying discarded on the road. He reached out his hand, took it, and killed a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With a donkey’s jawbone I have utterly destroyed them! With a donkey’s jawbone I have killed a thousand men!”
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand and named that place “Slaughter with the Jawbone.”
He became very thirsty and cried out to the Lord, saying, “You have granted this great deliverance through your servant’s hand. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
The Lord opened a hollow in that jawbone, and water came out of it. He drank, his spirit revived, and he recovered. For this reason that place has been called “Spring of the Jawbone” to this day.
He judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson went to Gaza, saw a prostitute there, and went in to her.

The people of Gaza were told, “Samson has come here.” They surrounded him and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They waited throughout the night, saying, “Let us wait for him until daybreak, and then we will kill him.”

Samson slept until midnight. At midnight he got up, seized the doors of the city gate with its two posts, and lifted them up together with all the [?]. He put them on his shoulders, carried them up to the top of the hill facing Hebron, and set them down there.
After this he fell in love with a woman by the river Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines went up to her and said, “Entice him and find out what gives him his great strength, and how we can overpower him and bind him so that we can subdue him. We will give you a thousand men [?] and a hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me what gives you your great strength, and what you could be bound with to make you weak.”
Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven new bowstrings that have never been broken, I will become weak and be like any other human being.”
The rulers of the Philistines brought her seven new bowstrings that had never been broken, and she bound him with them.

Men were waiting in ambush for him in the inner room. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” But he snapped those bowstrings as a thread snaps when fire touches it, and the source of his strength remained unknown.
Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Now tell me what you can be bound with.”
He said to her, “If they bind me with seven ropes that have never been used for any work, I will become weak and be like any other human being.”

Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” Men were waiting in ambush for him in the inner room, but he snapped the ropes off his arms like thread.

Delilah said to Samson, “Again you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Tell me what you can be bound with.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven locks of hair on my head and fasten them with a peg into the loom, I will become weak like any other human being.”

Delilah put him to sleep and tightly wove the seven locks of his head into the loom, fastening them with a peg. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and pulled the peg out of the loom along with his locks, and his strength was not discovered.
Delilah said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you, and my heart is with you’? This is now the third time you have mocked me and have not told me what gives you your great strength.”
Then, when she wore him down with her words all night and troubled him until he was distressed to the point of death,

he told her everything that was in his heart. He said to her, “No razor has touched my head, because I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God since I was in my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like any other human being.”

Delilah realized that he had told her everything that was in his heart. She sent and summoned the messengers of the Philistines, saying, “Come up once more, because he has told me everything that is in his heart.” All the rulers of the Philistines came up to her, bringing gold with them.
She put him to sleep between her knees and called a barber. She cut off the seven locks of his head, and he began to grow weak, and his strength left him.

Delilah said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and said, “I will go out and do as I always have, and shake them off.” But he did not know that the Lord had left him.
The Philistines seized him, put out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. They bound him with iron shackles and put him in prison to grind grain.
His hair began to grow again after they had shaved it off.
The leaders of the Philistines gathered to offer a sacrifice to their god and to celebrate. They said, “Our god has delivered Samson, our enemy, into our hands.”
When the people saw him, they praised their god and said, “Our god has delivered our enemy into our hands, the one who devastated our land and killed so many of us.”
Then, when they were celebrating, they said, “Call Samson out of prison, and let him entertain us.” They called Samson out of prison and mocked him, and they stood him between two pillars.
Samson said to the boy who was guiding him, “Let me rest, and let me feel the pillars on which this house stands, and let me lean against them.” The boy did this for him.
The building was full of men and women, and all the rulers of the Philistines were there. On the roof there were about three thousand men and women watching Samson entertain them.
Samson cried out to the Lord and said, “Lord, Lord, remember me and strengthen me just this once, so that I may take one act of vengeance on the Philistines for both my eyes.”
Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the building rested and pushed against them, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He forced the pillars with his strength, and the building fell on the rulers and on all the people inside it. Those whom Samson killed at his death were more numerous than those he had killed during his life.

His brothers and all his father’s household came down, took him, and brought him up. They buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.
He said to his mother, “That gold which you told me was stolen from you, and about which you swore an oath—look, the gold is with me. I took it.” His mother said, “May my son be blessed by the Lord.”

He returned the eleven hundred pieces of gold to his mother. His mother said, “I have solemnly dedicated this gold to the Lord from my own hands, for myself, to have a carved image and a cast image made.”

“And now I will return it to you and give it to you.” And he gave that gold to his mother. His mother took that gold and gave two hundred pieces of silver from it to someone who would melt it down and make it into a carved image. He melted it down, and they placed it in Micah’s house.
The man Micah made himself a house of God. He made an image and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days the Israelites had no king. Each person did what seemed right in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem, from the people of Judah and the clan of Judah. He was a Levite, and he lived there.
That man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to find somewhere to live. He reached the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house to spend the night.
Micah said to him, “Where have you come from?” He said to him, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am traveling to live wherever I find a place.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten loaves of bread each day, a set of clothes, and your food.” And that Levite went with him.
He began to live with that man, and the young man became like one of his sons.
Micah ordained that Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in Micah’s house.
Micah said, “Now I know that the Lord has treated me well, because a Levite has become my priest.”

In those days Israel had no king. In those days the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance for themselves where they could live, because until that time they had not received an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites sent five men from their tribe, from their own territory, capable men from Zorah and Eshtaol, to inspect the land and learn about it. They said to them, “Go and inspect the land for us.” They reached the hill country of Ephraim, came to Micah’s house, and stayed there at Micah’s house.
They recognized the voice of that young Levite. They went in there and said to him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing here? What do you have here?”
He said to them, “Micah has done this and that for me. He hired me, and I became his priest.”
They said to him, “Ask the Lord whether he will make the journey we are taking successful.”
The priest said to them, “Go in peace. The journey you are taking is before the Lord.”

Those men went and arrived at Laish. They saw that the people living there lived securely, according to the custom of Sidon, quiet and at ease, feeling safe. They could not speak a word in the land, [?] an inheritance of treasure, because they were far from Sidon and had no dealings with Syria.
Those five men returned to their fellow tribesmen in Zorah and Eshtaol, who said to them, “What is keeping you sitting there?”

“Get up, and let us go against it, because we entered that land and traveled through it to its boundaries. We saw the people who live in it according to the customs of Sidon. They are far from Sidon and have no dealings with Syria. But get up, and let us go up against them, because we have seen that the land is very good. Yet you remain silent! Do not be slow to go and enter and take possession of that land.
When you enter, you will come to a people who live securely, and the land is spacious. For the Lord has delivered into your hands a region that lacks none of the things produced on the earth.”
Six hundred men from the territory of Dan set out from there, from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed and carrying their weapons of war.
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. For this reason that place has been called the Camp of Dan to this day; it is behind Kiriath-jearim.
They passed on from there, reached the hill country of Ephraim, and came to Micah’s house.

The five men who had gone to inspect the land of Laish said to their brothers, “Do you know that in these houses there are an image, household gods, a carved idol, and a cast idol? Now consider what you should do.”
They turned aside there and entered the house of that young Levite, in Micah’s house.
The six hundred men of the Danites, carrying their weapons of war and fully armed, greeted him and gathered at the entrance of the gate.

The five men who had gone earlier to inspect the land went up, entered there, and took the image, the carved idol, the household gods, and the cast idol. The priest was standing at the entrance of the gate, while the seven hundred men were carrying their weapons of war, fully armed.
Those men entered Micah’s house and took the carved idol, the image, the household gods, and the cast idol. The priest said to them, “What are you doing?”

They said to him, “Be quiet! Put your hand over your mouth and come with us. Be our father and priest. Is it better for you to be priest to one man than to be priest to a tribe and a people of Israel?”
The priest’s heart was glad. He took the image, the household gods, the carved idol, and the cast idol, and went among the people.
They turned and went on their way. They took his whole household, his livestock, and his valuables, and put them ahead of them.
Before they had gone far from the house, Micah came with the men who lived near his house. They cried out behind the Danites and shouted to them.
The Danites turned around and said to Micah, “What is wrong with you, that you are shouting?”
Micah said to them, “You have taken away the carved idol I made, and my priest, and gone away. What have you left me? Yet you ask me, ‘Why are you shouting?’”
The Danites said to him, “Do not let your voice be heard among us again. Otherwise, bitter-tempered men may attack you, and you will lose your own life and the lives of your household.”
The Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, he turned back and returned to his house.
They took everything Micah had made, the priest, and everything he had, and went to Laish, against a peaceful people living securely. They killed them with the sword and burned their city.
No one escaped, because they were far from Sidon and had no dealings with other people. The city was in the valley belonging to Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and lived in it.
They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. Previously, the city’s name had been Laish.
The Danites set up Micah’s carved idol for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons served as priests for the people of Dan until the day their land went into exile.
They kept Micah’s carved idol, which he had made, set up for themselves throughout the time that the house of the Lord was in Shiloh.
In those days Israel had no king. There was a Levite living in one part of the hill country of Ephraim. This man took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
His concubine became angry with him, left him, and went to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. She stayed there for four months.

Her husband got up, went after her to be reconciled with her and bring her back to him, taking his servant and two donkeys with him. He went to her father’s house. When the girl’s father saw him, he went and welcomed him.
His father-in-law, the woman’s father, received him, and he stayed with him for three days. They ate and drank, and he spent the night there.
On the fourth day they woke early in the morning, and he got up to leave. The young woman’s father said to his son-in-law, “Strengthen yourself by eating a piece of bread, and then you may go.”
The two of them sat down and ate and drank together. The young woman’s father said to the man, “Spend tonight here too, and let your heart be glad.”
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law prevailed on him, and he spent another night there.
He woke early on the fifth day to leave. The young woman’s father said to him, “Eat some food, and then travel until the sun sets.” So the two of them ate and drank.

The man rose to leave with his concubine and his servant. His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, said to him, “Look, evening has come, and the sun is sinking. Spend tonight here too. Stay here and let your heart be glad. Tomorrow morning you can set out on your journey and go home.”
The man refused to stay overnight. He got up and went, and they arrived opposite Jebus, which is Jerusalem. He had two loaded donkeys with him, and his concubine was also with him.
While they were still opposite Jebus, the sun had sunk very low. The servant said to his master, “Come, let us turn aside into this city of the Jebusites and spend the night there.”
His master said to him, “We will not turn aside into a foreign city that does not belong to the Israelites. Let us go on to Gibeah.”
He said to his servant, “Come, let us turn aside into one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah of Ramah.”
They passed on and continued their journey until the sun set, when they reached Gibeah in Benjamin.
They turned aside there to enter Gibeah and spend the night. They entered and sat down in the city square, but no one took them into a house or gave them lodging.
