An old man came from his work. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim and lived in Gibeah, but the people of the place were Benjaminites.
He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square. The old man said to him, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?”

He said to him, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the hill country of Ephraim, for I come from there. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going home. But no one has taken me into his house.
We have straw and fodder for our donkeys. We also have bread and wine for ourselves, for your maidservant, and for the boy, your servants. We lack nothing that we need.”
The old man said to him, “Peace be with you. I will provide whatever you lack. Only do not spend the night in the square.”
He brought him into his house and gave feed to his donkeys. They washed their feet, ate, and drank.

Afterward, while their hearts were glad, wicked men of the city surrounded the house and pounded on the door. They said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came into your house so that we may have sex with him.”
The man who owned the house went out to them and said, “No, our brothers! Do not do evil. Since this man has entered my house, do not commit this outrage.”
“Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out. Humiliate them and do to them whatever seems good in your eyes, but do not do this outrageous thing to that man.”
Those men would not listen to him. The man took his concubine and brought her outside to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go when dawn broke.
The woman came in the morning and fell at the doorstep of the house belonging to the man where her master was staying. She lay there until daybreak.
Her master rose in the morning, opened the door of the house, and went out to continue his journey. He found his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, “Get up; let us go.” But she did not answer him, because she was dead. He loaded her onto a donkey, and the man set out and returned to his own country.
He entered his house, took a knife, seized his concubine, and cut her apart at the joints of her bones. He divided her into twelve pieces and sent her throughout the people of Israel.

Then everyone who saw her said, “Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen from the day Israel came out of Egypt until today.” He instructed the men whom he sent, saying to them, “Say this to all the people of Israel: ‘Has anything like this ever happened from the day the Israelites came out of Egypt until today? Consider it, take counsel, and speak.’”
All the Israelites went out and set forth, their whole congregation gathering as one man, from Dan to Beersheba, and also from Gilead, at Mizpah.
All the people and all the tribes of Israel stood in the assembly of all God’s people: four hundred thousand foot soldiers carrying spears.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah. The Israelites said, “Tell us how this evil happened.”
The Levite, the husband of the woman they had killed, answered, “My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah rose against us and surrounded the house that night. They wanted to kill me, and they humiliated and raped my concubine, and she died.
I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent them throughout the whole territory of Israel’s inheritance, because they had committed an outrage in Israel.
Now all of you are Israelites. Give your decision and advice here.”
All the people rose as one man and said, “We will not enter our houses or return to our dwellings.
Now do this against Gibeah: let us go up against them by lot.

Let us take ten men from every hundred throughout all the people of Israel, likewise a hundred from every thousand, and a thousand from every ten thousand, to carry provisions for the people on the journey—for those going to fight against Gibeah in Benjamin because of all the outrage they committed against Israel.”
All Israel gathered from their towns to go in.
The people of Israel sent messengers throughout the tribe of Benjamin, saying, “What is this evil that has happened among you?

Now hand over the men who sinned in Gibeah, the sons of Balaam, so that we may put them to death and remove evil from Israel.” But the Benjaminites refused to listen to their brothers, the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gathered from their towns at Gibeah to go out and fight against the Israelites.
That day the Benjaminites from their towns were counted: twenty-five thousand men carrying spears, besides those who lived in Gibeah.
Those were also counted: seven hundred chosen young men, all equally capable with either hand. All these were slingers who could sling a stone at a hair and split it without missing.
All the Israelites, apart from the Benjaminites, were counted: four hundred thousand men carrying spears. All these were fighting men.

They rose and went up to Bethel and inquired of the Lord. The Israelites said, “Who will go up as our leader to fight against Benjamin for us?” The Lord said to them, “Judah shall go up as your leader.”
The Israelites rose and camped against Gibeah.
All the men of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin and engaged them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of the town and killed twenty-two thousand Israelites that day, who fell to the ground.
The Israelites rallied and again went out to fight in the same place where they had fought on the first day.
The Israelites went up and wept before the Lord until evening. They inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall we again fight against Benjamin our brother?” The Lord said to them, “Go up against them.”
The Israelites came against Benjamin on the second day.
On the second day Benjamin came out of Gibeah to meet them and killed eighteen thousand of them, who fell to the ground. All of them carried spears.
All the Israelites and all the people went up to Bethel. They wept and sat there before the Lord. The people fasted until evening and offered peace offerings to the Lord.
The Israelites inquired of the Lord, and the ark of the Lord was there in those days.

Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, stood before it in those days. They asked, “Should we go out again to battle against the Benjaminites, our brothers, or should we stop?” The Lord told them, “Go up, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hands.”
The Israelites stationed men in ambush all around Gibeah.
On the third day Israel engaged Benjamin and fought against them near Gibeah as before.

The Benjaminites came out to meet the people and ran away from the city. As before, they began killing some of the people on the roads, one leading up to Bethel and the other leading up to Gibeah through the open country—about thirty men of Israel.
The Benjaminites said, “They are falling before us as before.” But the Israelites said, “Let us flee and draw them away from the city onto the roads.”
All the men of Israel rose from their positions and fought at Baal-tamar. Israel’s men in ambush also joined the fighting from their positions west of Gibeah.
Ten thousand chosen men from Israel came in front of Gibeah, and the fighting grew fierce. But the Benjaminites did not know that disaster had overtaken them.
The Lord struck down Benjamin before Israel, and the Israelites killed [?] Benjaminites. All of these were men who carried weapons.
Benjamin saw that they had been defeated. The Israelites had given ground to them because they trusted the men they had stationed in ambush against Gibeah.
Those who had been lying in ambush went forward and put the city to the sword.
Israel had instructed those lying in ambush to kill them with the sword and make the smoke of the city rise like a beacon.

The men of Israel turned back in the battle. As for Benjamin, they began killing the men of Israel, about six hundred men, for Benjamin said, “Before they kill me, I have killed them before me, as in the earlier battle.”
That beacon of smoke rose from the city like a pillar. Benjamin looked behind them, and there was the destruction of the city rising into the sky.
The men of Israel turned back, and the men of Benjamin were thrown into confusion and saw that disaster had overtaken them.
They fled before Israel along the road to the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. Those from the cities also killed them in their midst.
They killed the Benjaminites and destroyed them, utterly wiping them out before Gibeah, on its eastern side.
Eighteen thousand men from Benjamin fell, and all of these were strong warriors.
They turned and fled toward the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites cut down five thousand of them, pursued them, and followed them as far as Gideom, killing two thousand more of them.
All the Benjaminites who fell that day numbered twenty-five thousand men who carried weapons, all of them mighty warriors.
Six hundred men escaped and fled to the rock of Rimmon. They stayed at the rock of Rimmon for four months.
The men of Israel closed in on the Benjaminites and put them to the sword, along with their towns, their livestock, and everything found in the towns. They burned all the towns they came upon.
The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, saying, “None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjaminite.”
All the people went to Mizpah and to Bethel and remained before the Lord until evening. They cried out and wept bitterly.
They said, “Why, Lord, has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe should be lost from Israel?”
The next day the people rose early, built an altar there, and offered sacrifices of well-being.

The Israelites said, “Who among all the people of Israel did not come up to the assembly before the Lord?” For they had sworn a solemn oath, saying, “Anyone who did not come up before the Lord at Mizpah must surely be put to death.”
The Israelites were reconciled with Benjamin, their brother, and said, “Will one tribe be lost from Israel today?”
“What, then, shall we do about wives for those who remain? We ourselves have sworn by the Lord that we will not give them any of our daughters in marriage.”
They said, “Which of the tribes of Israel did not go up to the Lord at Mizpah?” And look, not a single man from Jabesh-gilead had come to their assembly.
They counted the people, and not a single man from Jabesh-gilead was present.
Their assembly sent twelve thousand valiant men there and commanded them, saying, “Go and kill everyone who lives in Jabesh-gilead with the sword, including the women and the rest of the people.”
“Do this: kill every male and every woman who has known a man.”
Among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead they found four hundred virgin girls who had not had sexual relations with a man. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.
The whole assembly sent messengers to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon and called them to make peace.
Benjamin returned to the Israelites in those days. They gave them wives from among the women of Jabesh-gilead, and they were pleased with this.
The people also felt sorry for Benjamin, because the Lord had caused slaughter among the people of Israel.
The leaders of the assembly said, “What shall we do about wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been destroyed?”
They said, “An inheritance remains for Benjamin, and no tribe must be wiped out from Israel.
But we cannot give them wives from among our daughters, because we Israelites swore an oath, saying, ‘Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin.’”
They said, “There is a yearly festival of the Lord at Shiloh, north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.”
They commanded the Benjaminites, saying to them, “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards.
Watch the daughters of the inhabitants of Shiloh as they dance to the lyre. Come out of the vineyards, seize wives for yourselves from among the daughters of Shiloh, and go into Benjamin.

If their fathers and brothers come to accuse you, we will tell them, ‘Have mercy on them, because they did not save their wives from the slaughter. It was not you who gave them wives at that time, so you need not repent.’”

The Benjaminites did so. They took wives to match their number, seizing them from among the women who were dancing. They went away and returned to their inheritance, built towns for themselves, and lived in them.
The Israelites departed from there, each to his own people and his own clan. They went away from there, each to his own inheritance.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.
